10027-the-triple-alliance-its-trials-and:
Harold Avery's school story follows a triple alliance of boys at Ronleigh College, beginning with a new boy and a clash with the Philistines. The alliance survives discomfiture, a supper club, catching a Tartar, and a gunpowder plot, all in the cheerful code of school fiction.

Later chapters bring third-form oratory, a holiday adventure, a screw loose in the sixth, the Wraxby match, and school elections. Avery writes for boys with high spirits and fair play. Readers get the classic boarding-school tale: friendship, mischief, sport, and the small triumphs that feel enormous at fourteen.
11372-the-nine-tenths:
James Oppenheim's 1911 novel The Nine-Tenths, dedicated to his father's memory, follows working New York through a printery, a hat factory, and a fire on East Eighty-First Street. Part one, The Dream, introduces Myra and Joe, Marty Briggs, and Joe Blaine's men; part two, The Test, follows the nine-tenths. others like Sally Heffer and Theodore Marrin, forty-five treacherous men, a fight, an arrest, a trial, and a workhouse, ending in confident morning and the city.

Oppenheim opens with hat-factory girls darting out for coffee and sandwiches, crowding a frail elevator with grimy pressmen, while oil-soaked cotton waste lies unnoticed in a dark corner. The novel's socialism is earnest: the nine-tenths who labor deserve the city they build. It remains a vivid document of Progressive-era labor fiction.
13942-brave-men-and-women-their-struggle:
O. E. Fuller published Brave Men and Women in 1884 as a book of inspiring lives. Its motto urges readers to find their fit work, labour hard at it, and keep a brave, honest heart. Chapters cover Benjamin Franklin, Sir Walter Scott and his mother, and Abigail Adams. Franklin's Poor Richard addresses taxes and thrift in homely wisdom.

Fuller defends Franklin against charges of meanness, quoting James Parton's answer. Scott's mother's education and domestic love shape her son's training. Adams appears as wife of the second president and mother of the sixth. The book mixes biography with moral exhortation. It suits readers who enjoy Victorian uplift and short lives.
14809-the-origin-and-deeds-of-the-goths:
Jordanes, a Christian Goth writing in 551, probably in Constantinople, recorded the origin and deeds of the Goths in his Getica. Charles C. Mierow's English version, part of a Princeton doctoral thesis in 1908, puts that story into English for the first time.

Mierow notes that readers who love the romance of history will enjoy a great tale of a lost cause, and will not mind the simple-hearted exaggerations of a eulogist of Gothic kings. From northern origins through migrations, battles and kingdoms, the narrative follows a people who shaped late Roman Europe. The translation remains a standard door into early Gothic history.
15774-ishmael-or-in-the-depths:
A long melodrama by Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth, author of The Hidden Hand and Self-Raised. A. L. Burt Company issued it in New York in handsome cloth at sixty cents. Southworth, a queen of popular romance, builds her tale on secrets, love, and fortune. Ishmael, a youth from the depths, rises through a world of plots and passions.

Hidden birth, lost kin, and rival lovers drive the huge plot through scene after scene. Virtue suffers, villainy schemes, and love at last finds its reward. Southworth writes with speed and feeling, never letting the reader rest. The novel charms as classic dime-novel romance: grand, tearful, and full of surprises at every turn.
16996-two-old-faiths:
J. Murray Mitchell and Sir William Muir wrote these 1891 essays on the religions of the Hindus and the Mohammedans, issued by the Chautauqua Press in New York. The essays were picked from the Present Day Tracts of the Religious Tract Society in London and reprinted by leave. A note warns that the Chautauqua council's recommendation does not mean approval of every principle in the book.

Mitchell and Muir set out Hindu and Muslim beliefs in outline, with chapters on gods, rites, and laws, from a Christian missionary standpoint. Their tone is earnest and scholarly for its day. The book gives a period survey of two great faiths, useful for history of religion, though modern readers will prefer later, insider accounts for depth and fairness.
18638-ideal-commonwealths:
Henry Morley edited this 1890 volume for Routledge's Universal Library, gathering five classic visions of a perfect state. It holds Plutarch's Lycurgus, Thomas More's Utopia, Francis Bacon's New Atlantis, and Tommaso Campanella's City of the Sun, with a fragment of Joseph Hall's Mundus Alter et Idem. Morley's introduction sets out Plato's Republic as the model behind them all.

Each work pictures a city ruled by fixed laws, shared goods, or wise guardians, yet each differs sharply in temper and detail. Read together, they show how writers across ages used an ideal city to judge their own times. The volume is a handy one-book tour of utopian thought.
22420-the-book-of-nature-myths:
The Book of Nature Myths retells tales that explain the natural world. Its opening story begins long ago, when the earth was very young. Two hunters travel through a forest far from home.

They have tracked a deer for many days by then. Night falls, dark and gloomy, around the hunters. Then a bright light comes in the western sky. Such a moment launches a myth of sky or star. The collection gathers such explanatory stories for young readers. Each tale answers a child's question about nature with a story. It preserves folk imagination in simple, clear retellings meant to be read aloud.
22518-quaint-epitaphs:
Quaint Epitaphs gathers curious inscriptions from gravestones into one book. Its compiler trusted readers would not call the book presumptuous. Many epitaph collections already existed when she published hers.

Requests for a look at her private collection prompted publication. Friends asked to examine it so often that printing followed. Graveyard verses preserve humor, grief, and local character in stone. A good epitaph can sum up a life in four lines. The compiler's haul comes from churchyards near and far. Readers get to wander cemeteries without leaving their chairs. The book charms by turns: funny, pious, odd, and sometimes deeply touching in brevity.
22693-a-book-of-myths:
A Book of Myths retells the great stories of Greek and other ancient myth for general readers. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Retellings of this era aimed to give children and busy adults the tales of gods and heroes in clear, handsome prose, with the worst crudities softened.

The sample's opening passage wrestles honestly with the gods' bad behavior. It wonders how heroes who fell fighting by the Scamander came to be worshipped as more than men. Such reflections frame the stories of Troy and Olympus that follow. The book belongs to the shelf of myth handbooks that formed the classical imagination of English-speaking readers. It still offers a graceful first path into the old tales.
23164-the-creature-from-cleveland-depths:
Fritz Leiber kicks a television in The Creature from Cleveland Depths. Gusterson gives the dead television a sour kick on his way past. If the company had use for them, he grumbles, it would pay them something. Wrong, his friend answers. Money never was the right goad for inner-directed men like Gussy, straight from the Motivations chief's own mouth.

Leiber sets his satire in a burrowed future Cleveland, where underground life runs on motivational jargon and gadgets that manage their owners. The creature of the title grows out of that managed world, part pet, part product, all consequence. Fay and Gussy argue their way through it in Leiber's wittiest register. The story predicts wearable masters with unnerving cheer, and remains very funny about a future that arrived on schedule.
24737-the-children-of-odin-the-book-of-n:
Padraic Colum wrote this book of northern myths, illustrated by Willy Pogany, retelling the Norse sagas for children. His rich, musical voice captures the magic of Asgard, the northern paradise of gods and goddesses before the dawn of history. All-Father Odin walks among men by way of the Rainbow Bridge.

Odin gives his right eye for a drink from Wisdom's well, Thor's hammer defends Asgard, and Loki's cunning turns him to treachery against the gods. Giants, dragons, dwarfs, and Valkyries crowd the tales, toward the last battle that destroyed their world. Young readers get a masterful telling of Norse myth.
2549-the-doom-of-the-griffiths:
Elizabeth Gaskell builds this Welsh tale around the traditions of Owen Glendower, the hero still loved by Welsh peasants, and a family shadowed by an old curse. The Griffiths of North Wales carry a doom that seems to follow their name from father to son.

Pride, violence, and a fatal inheritance drive the story toward its grim close, while Gaskell grounds the horror in real Welsh places and lore. The tale is short, dark, and full of the atmosphere of the hills. Readers get a folk tragedy that shows how a family's past can harden into fate.
26292-the-star-hyacinths:
James H. Schmitz's science-fiction story opens with a great unsolved crime: the robbery of the Dosey Asteroids shipping station. Raiders took six months of gem star hyacinths, worth near a hundred million credits, and seventy-nine station workers died. Most wounds were dealt to corpses, as if to hide a stranger disaster, and the dome locks had been opened from within.

Six years later, on a bleak, uncharted world, two wrecked ships lie near a lake arm. A lone man gazes at a star hyacinth whose brilliance burns his sight, and searchers spot smoke rising near the wrecks. Names such as Leed Farous, Duomart, and Dr. Egavine enter as the mystery of the gems and the dead station starts to close.
5636-winding-paths:
Gertrude Page wrote Winding Paths as a novel about Dudley Pritchard, a hard-working London architect, and his lively young sister Hal. Fifteen years separate them, and Dudley views with alarm Hal's friendship with Lorraine Vivian, a fully fledged actress. He disapproved of Lorraine from their first meeting, for no particular reason, as he disapproved of many things without troubling to find out why.

Hal, still a hoydenish schoolgirl, understands her brother far better than he understands her, finding humor in his self-congratulatory tolerance. The novel follows siblings, theatre folk, and London society. Readers get an engaging Edwardian story of family, judgment, and young independence.
6376-self-raised-or-from-the-depths:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth opens Self Raised, or From the Depths, with recovery and a verse on hope darkened by doubt. Ishmael, parted from Claudia in anguish, will not long succumb to despair, for his strength of intellect and will holds him, and Bee's love holds him too. Bee has loved him since school, through country teaching and law study, and loves him now as a successful barrister, while Claudia's power to desolate his life has limits.

Chapters run from Herman and Ishmael and second love through Woodside and Tanglewood. A professor of odd jobs, a journey, and Lady Vincent's reception follow. Romance and reality, Castle Cragg, Faustina, and a plot against Claudia follow, with a judge sailing from Boston on the Oceana and Ishmael agreeing to go, whatever sacrifices it costs. Southworth writes melodrama with moral force, where a self raised man rises by work and loyalty.
6561-our-friend-john-burroughs:
Clara Barrus writes of John Burroughs as a friend, not just as a writer of books on birds and fields. Her chapters follow him from his farm boyhood and family life to his days at Slabsides, his winter walks, and his camps with John Muir. Sketches of his early work sit beside warm, close glimpses of the man himself.

Barrus notes how praise in a man's own time can feel uneasy, and how true worth shows only with years. Yet her tone stays fond, not stiff, as she recalls talk, walks, and quiet hours outdoors. Our Friend John Burroughs gives a personal portrait of a poet of nature, seen by one who knew him well.
7291-the-two-paths:
John Ruskin's Two Paths gathers five lectures on art and its power over nations. They open with the deteriorative power of conventional art. Then they move through the unity of art, modern manufacture and design, the influence of imagination in architecture, and the work of iron in nature, art, and policy. Appendices and a list of illustrations, from the ideal of an angel to the serpent beguiling Eve, support the text.

Ruskin argues that art shapes a people's character for good or ill, and that honest making beats empty ornament every time. His lectures, spoken at different times yet linked by design, preach with a prophet's heat and a craftsman's eye. The book remains a fierce, eloquent plea for truth in art and work.
9250-a-book-of-autographs:
Hawthorne's Book of Autographs considers a volume of letters, chiefly by soldiers and statesmen of the Revolution, addressed to General Palmer, himself a swordsman for the cause. They suit a quiet afternoon, withdrawn from the present, when a reader can glide back three quarters of a century and stand amid ominous circumstances.

Imagine the letters just brought by a splashed postrider or a hurried dragoon, Hawthorne urges, and they become magic scrolls. The sketch meditates on handwriting as character. It remains a charming essay on history made personal by ink and paper.
9855-classic-myths:
Mary Catherine Judd, principal of the Lincoln School in Minneapolis, retold Classic Myths for young readers, with pictures by Angus MacDonall drawn from classic sources. Tales span Greek, Norse, Roman, German, Finnish, and Russian lore. The sun's horses, Woden of the northern sky, and Jupiter of the southern sky open the set. Diana, Jack and Jill on the moon mountains, and the man in the moon follow.

Later myths tell how fire came to earth, why rivers hold gold sands, and how Echo, Iris, and Neptune rule air and sea. Judd writes with plain clarity for school use. A reader gets a wide, gentle book of world myths, fit for reading aloud and first wonder.
c-f-meyer-die-hochzeit-des-monchs:
A monk leaves his monastery for love, and the consequences unfold like a dark fairy tale in C. F. Meyer's Die Hochzeit des Moenchs, given here in German. The Monk's Wedding is framed as a story told at Dante's tomb in Verona, which lends the telling a solemn music. Passion stands against vows throughout the novella.

The frame's listeners interrupt, question, and darken the tale as it proceeds, a device Meyer handles beautifully. Medieval atmosphere thickens around a very modern psychology of desire and guilt. The monk's choice echoes outward until no one in the story stands untouched. Haunting is the word readers reach for with this one. It shows the master's late manner at full strength.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-cloths:
Altar cloths cover the altar during the Mysteries, as St. Optatus of Mileve notes in the fourth century. A law attributed to Boniface III in the seventh century made the covering obligatory, and three cloths became customary probably in the ninth, now strictly required for a licit Mass. The rule guards against spilt Precious Blood reaching the altar stone, since the cloths absorb it first.

Formally cloths were gold and silver cloth set with stones, silk, and other rich material, but now only linen or hemp may be used. The two lower cloths have to cover the whole table, length and width, whether one folded piece or two distinct pieces. The top cloth stays single and reaches the predella on both sides. Celebrating without a cloth is a grievous offence except in grave necessity, such as Sunday Mass or Viaticum for the dying.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andechs:
Andechs is a Benedictine monastery and pilgrimage place on a hill east of the Ammersee in Upper Bavaria. Its site first held a castle of the counts of Diessen, probably Roman. Pilgrimage fame dates from 955. Relics Saint Rasso had brought from Rome and the East to Worth were moved here to escape the Huns.

In the twelfth century three Sacred Hosts joined the relics. Two were reputedly consecrated by Gregory I, one by Leo IX. Andechs became Der heilige Berg, the holy mountain. A thirteenth-century Andechs missal in Munich gives the earliest mention of the Hosts. Duke Ernest raised a collegiate church in 1438. Duke Albert III turned it into a Benedictine monastery in 1455, with monks from Tegernsee. It became an abbey in 1458. Prosperity ran until secularization in 1803. In 1850 it rose again as a Benedictine priory under Munich's Saint Boniface abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casimir-ubagh:
Casimir Ubaghs was born at Bergélez-Fauquemont in November 1800 and died at Louvain in February 1875. For a quarter century he led the Ontologico-Traditionalist School of Louvain. After teaching philosophy at Rolduc, he moved to Louvain in 1830, and the school became a center of Ontologism under him. In 1846 he took over the Revue catholique, the school's official journal, with Arnold Tits and Lonay, drawing followers such as La Forêt, Claessens, Bouquillon, and Van Loo.

Opponents led by Kersten's Journal historique et littéraire fought the Revue for years, with the fiercest controversy from 1858 to 1861. The Index had already flagged five propositions in 1843 and ordered corrections Ubaghs misunderstood. A Roman Congregation decision of September 1864 censured a series of his Ontologism propositions, ending his career. His books include a natural theology in four editions, anthropology texts, and an 1860 essay on ontological ideology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-post-:
English post-Reformation oaths are the subject of this entry, which explains why the Crown demanded them. Since the Reformation was imposed from above, submission to its key formulas was exacted by oath, test, or formal declaration, and the formulas shifted with the moods of those in power. The oath of royal supremacy, imposed in March 1534, stands first.

The title Supreme Head had entered a convocation decree in February 1531 and met stiff clerical resistance, since it might later gain a religious sense it did not yet carry. On the advice of Fisher and Warham, the clergy submitted after adding the saving words, as far as God's law allows. Two years later Parliament declared the king the only supreme head on earth of the Church of England. Fisher and More would accept the succession of Anne Boleyn's children but refused the supremacy, and paid for that refusal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomuk Fuchs was a Bavarian chemist and mineralogist whose name still attaches to soluble glass. Born in 1774, he first studied medicine, then turned to chemistry and mineralogy at Heidelberg, Berlin, Freiburg, and Paris. He taught at Landshut and Munich, joined the Academy of Sciences in 1823, and became conservator of Munich's mineral museum in 1854.

His best-known discovery, published in 1823, was water glass, an alkaline silicate used in a kind of fresco painting called stereochromy and later in surgical bandages. He also worked on cement, the artificial production of ultramarine, beet sugar, brewing, and dyeing, and a chromium-bearing variety of muscovite was named fuchsite after him. His collected works appeared at Munich in 1856, the year of his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oaths:
An oath, in moral theology, asks God to stand witness to a statement’s truth, directly by his name or indirectly by creatures that show his majesty. Swearing by heaven, the cross, or the Gospels counts as tacit invocation, and every oath needs at least a virtual intent to invoke God's testimony.

The entry sorts oaths into assertory, affirming past or present fact, and promissory, binding a future resolve, vow, or pact. Contestatory oaths merely invoke witness, imprecatory ones add a curse on falsehood, and the entry weighs when oaths bind, when they excuse, and when they sin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostrogoths:
The Ostrogoths were one of the Goths' two chief tribes, a Germanic folk. Their oldest homes on record stood on the right bank of the Vistula. About the middle of the second century they moved, in whole or in part, to the Black Sea lands between the Don and Danube. From there they raided Greek and Asian cities and fought Romans and neighbour tribes without rest.

Emperor Decius fell against them in 251, and after defeat by Claudius in 269 they held Dacia from Aurelian. United under Ermanaric from 350 to 375, they fell to the Huns, then won freedom when Attila's empire broke in 453. Theodoric later ruled Italy with Roman law, art, and letters, tolerant toward Catholics though Arian himself. His kingdom fell in a long war, and the last Ostrogoth fortress fell in 555.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-special-devot:
Special devotions for months grew out of the slow separation of popular prayer from the official liturgy. And this entry explains the shift and then lists the devotions month by month. In the Middle Ages laity joined the daily psalmody, Mass. And processions and knew the liturgy well, while extra practices like the Rosary, a stand-in for the 150 Psalms, still sprang from liturgical roots.

From the sixteenth century onward, unliturgical practices took their own course, with Stations of the Cross, Forty Hours, litanies, novenas, and series of Sundays for particular saints or mysteries. Whole months came to belong to one devotion, January to the Holy Name of Jesus among them, and the entry pairs each month's devotion with its indulgences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-griffi:
Thomas Griffiths, Vicar Apostolic of the London District, was born in London in 1791 and died in 1847, the only holder of that office educated wholly in England. Sent to St. Edmund's College, Old Hall, at thirteen, he was ordained in 1814 and chosen president at twenty-seven, ruling the college with success for fifteen years. Consecrated Bishop of Olena in 1833, he succeeded Bishop Bramston three years later.

His years in office saw the first stirrings of the hierarchy's restoration and the subdivision of England's four districts into eight in 1840. The Oxford conversions followed, with Newman a Catholic nearly two years before Griffiths died. Irish immigration after the potato famine forced many new missions, and Pugin's revival of Christian art was gathering pace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-visigoths:
The Visigoths were one of the two principal branches of the Goths, sharing history with the Ostrogoths until 375. Ulfilas laboured among them, translated the Bible into their tongue, and preached Arianism with great success until Prince Athanaric forced him to withdraw in 348. At the Huns' invasion some fled with Athanaric to Transylvania's mountains, but most appealed to Emperor Valens to enter the Roman Empire.

In 376 some 200,000 Visigoths crossed the Danube, revolted against oppressive governors, plundered the country, and defeated and killed Valens near Adrianople in 378. Theodosius made peace in 382, seeking to unite them with the empire through national commanders and to reconcile Arians with Nicene Christians. After his death in 395 they elected Alaric of the Baltha family king. Sought a Germanic kingdom on Roman soil, invaded the Balkans to the Peloponnese in 396, and entered Italy in 401.
govdocs-archive_org-KlausFuchs_Klaus_Fuc: An FBI records-review inventory sheet for the New York files logs the bureau's holdings on Klaus Fuchs. Fuchs was the physicist who spied for the Soviet Union from inside the atomic bomb project. Review sheets record what a file holds and where its parts were sent, here between the Bureau and Albuquerque among others. He confessed in 1950. The sheet is pure paperwork: declassified inventory from the handling of the Cold War's most damaging espionage case.
our-friend-john-burroughs:
Clara Barrus, physician and devoted friend of the naturalist John Burroughs, assembled Our Friend John Burroughs as a contemporary tribute rather than a posthumous life. Its contents mix her own framing with his autobiographical sketches. Ancestry, childhood, self-analysis, and the early writings appear. So do a winter day at his Slabsides cabin, and camping with John Muir.

Everyone claims Burroughs as a friend, Barrus begins, because he is blended with our love of birds, flowers, and the outdoors. Against the obituary method of appreciation — wait until the daisies have bloomed over a man for decades — she offers familiar glimpses now, from readers who walked and listened beside him. The book preserves the poet-naturalist as his own generation knew him.
self-raised-or-from-the-depths:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth wrote this long novel of a lowly hero raised by his own worth. Contents run past thirty-eight chapters, moving from Recovery and Father and Son through journeys, storms, and a shipwreck. Names in the chapter heads include Herman, Ishmael, Bee, and Claudia.

Plots against Claudia, a night of horror in a castle vault, and a rescue late in the book promise rich sensation. Southworth blends love, pride, and hidden birth in the lush style her serial readers loved. The tale rewards patience with reversals at every turn, as worth wins out over rank and malice.
the-doom-of-the-griffiths:
Elizabeth Gaskell's tale The Doom of the Griffiths grows from Welsh lore about Owen Glendower. Gaskell opens with her own love of North Wales traditions and notes that Glendower lives in folk memory as much for magic as for patriot pride. A prize poem at Oxford on his name once stirred the whole principality, she says.

At its heart stands a curse. Glendower spared a false friend who plotted his death, and doomed his line instead. The Griffiths family bears that doom down the years. Gaskell blends folk tale, history, and moral weight.
the-nine-tenths:
James Oppenheim's novel The Nine-Tenths, dated 1911 and dedicated to the memory of his father, is present here only in title page, dedication, and contents, so the story does not appear. The contents divide the novel into two parts, The Dream and The Test, each with its own numbered chapters.

Part I opens in The Printery, then turns to The East Eighty-First Street Fire and The Good People. Myra and Joe, Marty Briggs, and Last of Joe Blaine and His Men follow. Part II promises beginnings, a chapter sharing the book's title, forty-five treacherous men, a fight in good earnest, an arrest, and The Trial, with a character named Rhona entering late.
the-origin-and-deeds-of-the-goths:
Jordanes, a Christian Goth, wrote the Getica, the origin and deeds of his people, in the year 551, probably at Constantinople. Charles C. Mierow put the work into English as part of his Princeton doctoral thesis, published in 1908. A note by Andrew F. West says this is the first time the Gothic story appears in English form.

West warns that Jordanes mixes fable and legend with fact and praises his own race freely. Readers who want cold, scientific narrative, he says, should stay away. Yet he calls the tale a great story of a lost cause, and its simple-hearted exaggerations heighten rather than spoil its interest for lovers of the romance of history.
the-triple-alliance-its-trials-and-trium: Harold Avery's Triple Alliance, Its Trials and Triumphs, is a school story presented here by its contents list alone. Twenty chapters begin with A New Boy and the Philistines, then move through a supper club, catching a Tartar, a gunpowder plot, and Ronleigh College. Later headings promise the Wraxby match, elections, a reading-room riot, a cipher letter Diggory reads, and a secret society. The alliance's trials can be followed in outline here, while its members speak only beyond this record.
the-two-paths: John Ruskin's Two Paths is laid out here in a contents list and a list of illustrations, stopping at the heading of his preface. Five lectures are promised. They cover the deteriorative power of conventional art over nations, and the unity of art. Modern manufacture and design follow. So do imagination in architecture, and the work of iron in nature, art, and policy. The illustrations name an angel, the serpent beguiling Eve, and classical architecture. Ruskin's lectures are charted here, while his arguments begin past the preface heading.
two-old-faiths: Two Old Faiths offers essays on the religions of the Hindus and the Mohammedans by J. Murray Mitchell and Sir William Muir. The Chautauqua Press at New York issued the book in 1891 for the C.L.S.C. reading circles. The essays were selected from the Religious Tract Society's Present Day Tracts. The contents begin the Hindu essay with the Vedas, philosophy, and ritualism. Only the title pages and start of the contents are present here, so the essays themselves do not appear.
winding-paths: Gertrude Page's Winding Paths is represented here by its title page and a bare contents list, so nothing of the story can be seen. The contents name no chapter titles at all. Forty-three chapters are listed by number alone, from chapter one to chapter forty-three. No place, person, or event is named in the pages present. Readers learn the author's name, the book's title, and its length in chapters, and nothing more of what the paths wind through or where they lead.
